1. Accessory-Rail Installation  
   • Purpose: Provides standardized mounting points (Picatinny, Weaver or M-LOK) for optics, lights, lasers and bipods on the firearm’s receiver or handguard.  
   • Process Overview:  
     – Layout and Marking: The installer measures and marks the exact position on the handguard or frame where the rail section will sit, ensuring alignment with the bore axis.  
     – Milling or Slot Cutting: Using a horizontal mill or dedicated slotting jig, a channel is cut to match the rail’s base profile. Depth and width are controlled to factory specifications (typically 20 mm wide for Picatinny).  
     – Rail Attachment: The rail is seated into the machined slot and secured with high-grade screws or T-nuts torqued to the manufacturer’s spec. Some systems use captive nuts or sliding T-slots.  
     – Final Alignment Check: A sighting tool or bore-sighting laser confirms that the rail is co-axial with the barrel.  

2. Barrel Threading for Muzzle Devices  
   • Purpose: Creates male threads on the barrel’s muzzle to accept flash hiders, compensators, muzzle brakes or thread protectors.  
   • Process Overview:  
     – Pre-Cut Preparation: The barrel is secured in a straight-turning lathe chuck or collet, ensuring concentricity with the lathe’s axis.  
     – Measuring Thread Specifications: The target thread diameter (for example, ½×28 TPI on many pistol barrels or 5/8×24 on .30-cal rifles) and thread pitch are confirmed.  
     – Cutting Operation: A form-tool or single-point threading tool is advanced into the rotating barrel at the correct lead angle. Multiple passes are taken, each removing a small amount until full thread depth is reached.  
     – Chamfering and Crowning: A slight chamfer is added at the muzzle to ease device installation, and the very end of the bore is re-crowned (often with a 90° or 11°/12° angle cutter) to preserve accuracy.  

3. Grip Panel or Stock Swaps (and Stippling)  
   • Purpose: Alters ergonomics and surface texture without changing any serialized component. Common in handguns and long guns alike.  
   • Process Overview:  
     – Disassembly: Stocks or grip panels are removed by taking out their mounting screws or bolts from the frame or receiver.  
     – Fitting: After dry-fitting the new panels or stock (often made of polymer, wood or composite), minimal material is sanded off mating surfaces to achieve a seamless fit.  
     – Installation: Panels are torqued down per the manufacturer’s guidance. Free-floating stocks add hardware like QD sling sockets or cheek risers using the same bolt holes.  
     – Optional Stippling/Texturing: On polymer grips, a heated soldering-iron tip or dedicated stippling tool melts tiny pits in the surface. Patterns range from checkerboards to aggressive “gator” scales.  

4. Slide or Receiver Milling (Serrations, Fluting, Lightening Cuts)  
   • Purpose: Enhances slide/receiver appearance, reduces reciprocating mass, or adds tactile serrations for slide manipulation.  
   • Process Overview:  
     – Fixturing: The slide (or upper receiver) is locked in a precision fixture on a vertical or horizontal CNC mill. Alignment pins ensure the bore and rail interfaces remain square to the cutter.  
     – CAD/Toolpath Setup: A 3D model or drawing of the desired cuts—serrations at front and rear, angled ports, flutes running lengthwise or cut-outs for weight reduction—is loaded into CAM software.  
     – Machining: Carbide end mills (often 1/8″ to 1/4″ diameter) execute the programmed toolpaths. Speeds, feeds and depth-per-pass are optimized for the material (e.g., stainless steel vs. forged aluminum).  
     – Deburring and Edge Blending: After cutting, all sharp edges are hand-filed or tumbled to remove burrs and soften corners.  

5. External Surface Finishes (Cerakote, Anodizing, Hydrographics)  
   • Purpose: Alters the external appearance and corrosion resistance of metal and polymer parts.  
   • Process Overview:  
     – Complete Disassembly & Cleaning: All components are stripped of oils, coatings and contaminants via ultrasonic cleaning, chemical baths or bead blasting.  
     – Masking: Threads, bearing surfaces and internal bores are masked off with heat-resistant tape or plugs.  
     – Primer or Pre-Treatment: For Cerakote, a proprietary adhesion promoter is applied; for anodizing, parts enter an acid bath that builds oxide layers.  
     – Color Application:  
       • Cerakote: Thin layers of ceramic-polymer are applied by HVLP spray. Multiple coats (often two to three) build uniform coverage.  
       • Anodizing: Electric current induces oxide growth; dyes may be introduced to impart color before a sealing step locks in the finish.  
       • Hydrographics: A printed film floats on water; dipping the part transfers the pattern.  
     – Curing or Sealing: Cerakote parts are baked in an oven at a specified temperature and time. Anodized parts may be sealed in hot water or nickel-acetate.  
     – Final Inspection: Coating thickness is measured (e.g., with a magnetic film gauge), and adhesion is tested by cross-hatch or tape pull tests.
